body:
The Funen, on the site of Zeeburg, the city bastion that survived longest, was planned in 2000 by Frits van Dongen of Architecten Cie as sixteen separate blocks in a car-free park, each with its own design, by nine architects in all. NL Architects' Blok K, known as Verdana, was the last of them, completed in 2009.

The rules said three storeys, with half of the top floor a roof terrace. The architects read that as a block 7.5 metres high, then started pushing. They turned the central access lane slightly so it runs diagonally, which gave every house a different footprint and opened a shortcut through the block. To keep each of the ten houses at the same volume, 633 cubic metres, the short ones grew taller and the long ones lower, from one and a half to four storeys. The result is the rolling roof, covered in moss and sedum, with terraces poking out at seemingly random spots.

Because front doors and storage sit on that inner lane, the fronts facing the park could be largely glass. The houses are private; the park around them is open to all.

Look for:
- the rolling sedum roof
- the gold-coloured window frames
- the diagonal lane through the middle
